title: Coupling features link to clinical burden (frailty, allostatic load)
statement: Dynamic coupling features are associated with systemic clinical burden markers (frailty index, allostatic load, homeostatic dysregulation) after adjusting for age and site, indicating that inter-organ coupling disruption reflects whole-body physiological deterioration.
mechanism: Frailty, allostatic load, and homeostatic dysregulation are integrative measures of cumulative physiological damage across multiple organ systems. If inter-organ coupling (glucose-HR, glucose-activity) reflects the functional integrity of regulatory feedback loops, then coupling disruption should correlate with these burden markers because both arise from the same underlying process: progressive failure of multi-system homeostatic coordination.
predictions: Glucose-HR awake correlation is positively associated with frailty index after adjusting for age and site
Glucose multiscale entropy is associated with allostatic load
Glucose-activity coupling is associated with homeostatic dysregulation
Associations survive adjustment for age and site

literature.title: Network physiology reveals relations between network topology and physiological function
literature.key_finding: Inter-organ coupling topology reflects physiological state.
literature.relevance: Supports the link between coupling disruption and systemic physiological deterioration.

feasibility.statistical_power: N~1900 provides excellent power for partial correlations of r~0.15
key_challenges: Frailty index and allostatic load construction requires multiple clinical variables
dataset_limitations: Cross-sectional design prevents determining if coupling disruption precedes or follows clinical burden accumulation

test_plan.primary_method: Partial correlation between coupling features and clinical burden markers, adjusted for age and site, with FDR correction
implementation_steps: Construct frailty index, allostatic load, and homeostatic dysregulation scores from clinical data
Compute partial correlations between each coupling feature and each burden marker
Apply FDR correction across all tests
test_plan.time_window: Full 10-day overlap for coupling; clinical measures at enrollment
test_plan.success_criterion: FDR-significant partial correlations between at least one coupling feature and each burden marker
test_plan.refutation_criterion: No FDR-significant associations after age/site adjustment

results.method_used: Partial correlation with FDR correction, adjusted for age and site
results.interpretation: Dynamic coupling features are significantly associated with all three systemic burden markers. Glucose-HR coupling links to frailty, glucose entropy links to allostatic load, and glucose-activity coupling links to homeostatic dysregulation. This suggests coupling disruption is a general marker of physiological deterioration, not specific to glycemic control alone.

issues: Partial correlations of r~0.15 are statistically significant but explain only ~2% of variance
May be confounded by diabetes severity driving both coupling and burden
confounders_missed: Diabetes severity group as potential confounder
suggestions: Test whether coupling-burden associations persist within diabetes severity strata
Use structural equation modeling to separate direct and mediated paths

notes: Coupling features link to systemic burden markers, supporting their interpretation as general physiological deterioration indicators rather than purely glycemic markers.
